summary: Describes version 2 of the Internet Key Exchange protocol, used in IPsec for mutual authentication and for creating and maintaining security associations. It combines several earlier documents, including ISAKMP, IKE, the DOI, NAT traversal, legacy authentication, and remote address acquisition. IKEv2 does not interoperate with version 1 but can share the same UDP port. It was later replaced by RFC 5996.

eli5.summary: Before two computers send secret messages, they need to agree on keys. IKEv2 is the handshake where they prove who they are and agree on the secret.

questions: how does ipsec key exchange work
how does ikev2 differ from ikev1
why does ikev2 use udp port 4500
subtitle: Version 2 of the IPsec key exchange: four messages to authenticate both sides and set up encrypted tunnels.

tldr.problem: IPsec traffic needs shared state between the two ends, such as which algorithms to use and which keys, and setting that up by hand does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: IKEv2 runs request and response exchanges over UDP. An IKE_SA_INIT exchange negotiates algorithms and does a Diffie-Hellman exchange, and an IKE_AUTH exchange authenticates both sides and creates the first child security association for ESP or AH. Later exchanges create more child SAs or do housekeeping.
tldr.outcome: IKEv2 merges ISAKMP, IKE and the Internet DOI (RFC 2407, 2408 and 2409) along with NAT traversal, legacy authentication and remote address acquisition. This RFC has itself been obsoleted by RFC 5996.

today: RFC 4306 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 5996 and updated by RFC 5282. Use the newer specification for current work. It replaced RFC 2407, RFC 2408 and RFC 2409.

sections.title: The Initial Exchanges
sections.content:
IKE is the part of IPsec that performs mutual authentication and creates and maintains security associations (SAs). This document, RFC 4306, defines version 2 and is meant to replace RFC 2407, RFC 2408 and RFC 2409. The IKE SA is called the IKE_SA, and the SAs it sets up for ESP or AH are called CHILD_SAs.

All IKE traffic is made of request and response pairs called exchanges. The first pair, IKE_SA_INIT, negotiates cryptographic algorithms, exchanges nonces and does a Diffie-Hellman exchange. The second pair, IKE_AUTH, exchanges identities and optional certificates, proves knowledge of the secrets for those identities, and sets up the first CHILD_SA. Parts of these messages are encrypted and integrity protected with keys from the first exchange, so identities are hidden from eavesdroppers.

After that, either side may start a CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange to make another child SA or to rekey, or an INFORMATIONAL exchange to delete SAs, report errors or check liveness. The RFC describes three typical scenarios: gateway to gateway, endpoint to endpoint, and endpoint to gateway (for example a roaming laptop reaching a corporate network).
sections.eli5: First the two computers agree on a secret code, then they show each other their ID cards, and then they open a safe tunnel. After that they can open more tunnels or ask each other simple questions like 'are you still there?'.

sections.title: Reliability, Cookies, Rekeying and Negotiation
sections.content:
IKE normally uses UDP port 500, and also port 4500. Because UDP is unreliable, the initiator of each request is responsible for retransmitting it, and retransmission times MUST increase exponentially. Every message carries a 32-bit Message ID that matches responses to requests and detects retransmissions. By default an endpoint waits for each response before sending the next request, unless the peer has sent a SET_WINDOW_SIZE notification. All implementations MUST handle IKE messages up to 1280 bytes, and SHOULD handle messages up to 3000 bytes, because IKE has no fragmentation of its own.

To resist floods of forged start-up requests, a responder under load SHOULD answer an initial message with a COOKIE notification instead of keeping state. The initiator must then repeat its request with the cookie included, which shows it can receive packets at its claimed address. The RFC gives an example cookie built from a hash of the initiator nonce, address, SPI and a secret that the responder changes periodically.

Algorithm negotiation uses proposals made of protocols, transforms and attributes, and the responder MUST accept exactly one proposal. If the initiator guessed the wrong Diffie-Hellman group, the responder replies with INVALID_KE_PAYLOAD, and the initiator retries with its full list of suites, since the rejection was unauthenticated. SAs are rekeyed by creating a new SA and then deleting the old one, and in IKEv2 each end enforces its own lifetime rather than negotiating one.

An endpoint MUST NOT decide a peer has failed based on unprotected messages such as ICMP or unauthenticated Notify messages. This keeps IKE usable during denial of service attacks.
sections.eli5: If somebody sends a lot of fake knocks on a door, the host asks each visitor to repeat a special word before opening it. IKE does the same with a cookie so the host does not waste effort on pranksters.

sections.title: The IKE Header and Payloads
sections.content:
Each IKE message starts with a header and is followed by one or more payloads, each naming the next one in a Next Payload field. On port 4500 the message is preceded by four zero octets that are not part of the IKE message. The header holds two 8-octet SPIs, the version numbers, the exchange type, flags, a 4-octet Message ID and a 4-octet length. The Major Version is 2 and the Minor Version is 0 for this document.

The Exchange Type is 34 for IKE_SA_INIT, 35 for IKE_AUTH, 36 for CREATE_CHILD_SA and 37 for INFORMATIONAL. The I flag is set in messages from the original initiator and the R flag marks a response. An Encrypted payload MUST be the last payload in a packet.

Payloads include SA, Key Exchange, Identification, Certificate, Certificate Request, Authentication, Nonce, Notify, Delete, Vendor ID, Traffic Selector, Encrypted, Configuration and EAP. For forward compatibility, a payload header carries a critical flag, and a message with an unrecognized critical payload MUST be rejected.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with an envelope that says who is talking, which step it is, and how long the letter is. The letter inside is split into labelled pages.

sections.title: Keys and Authentication
sections.content:
All keying material comes from the negotiated pseudo-random function (prf), applied repeatedly in a construction called prf+. From the nonces and the Diffie-Hellman shared secret, each side computes SKEYSEED, and from that seven secrets: SK_d for deriving child SA keys, SK_ai and SK_ar for integrity, SK_ei and SK_er for encryption, and SK_pi and SK_pr for building AUTH payloads. The two directions use different keys. Child SA keys come from SK_d and the nonces, and from a fresh Diffie-Hellman value if one is included.

Each peer authenticates by signing, or computing a MAC over, the first message it sent or received plus the other side's nonce, so each side signs the other's nonce. Peers can use public key signatures with certificates, or a shared secret. The RFC warns that deriving a shared secret from a user-chosen password is typically insecure because dictionary attacks are not prevented.

IKE also supports the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP). The initiator leaves out the AUTH payload in the third message and the exchange continues with EAP messages. EAP is used for the initiator, and the responder MUST still authenticate with a public key signature.
sections.eli5: The two sides mix their secret numbers into a shared secret that nobody watching can work out. From it they cut separate keys for each job, like a different key for each door. Then each proves who they are by signing the other's random number.

sections.title: NAT Traversal, Addresses and Conformance
sections.content:
Network address translators (NATs) break IPsec in several ways, so IKEv2 can negotiate UDP encapsulation of IKE and ESP packets on port 4500. Both sides include NAT_DETECTION_SOURCE_IP and NAT_DETECTION_DESTINATION_IP notifications in the IKE_SA_INIT exchange to find out whether a NAT is on the path. If a NAT is found, all later IKE and ESP traffic for that IKE_SA goes over port 4500. NAT traversal support is optional.

A remote client can ask the gateway for an internal address by including a Configuration payload (CP) in the IKE_AUTH exchange. The reply can carry the address, netmask and other attributes. IKEv2 also requires ECN to be usable on the outer IP headers of tunnel-mode SAs.

Minimal implementations are allowed. Optional features include NAT traversal, temporary address requests, legacy authentication, window sizes above one, multiple SAs in one IKE_SA, and rekeying. Every implementation MUST be able to do the four-message exchange and answer an INFORMATIONAL exchange. To conform, it MUST be configurable to accept PKIX certificates with RSA keys of 1024 or 2048 bits and shared-key authentication.
sections.eli5: Some routers rewrite the address on your envelope, which confuses the secret-tunnel setup. IKEv2 wraps its messages in an extra envelope that these routers handle gracefully.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The initiator has to identify itself and usually authenticate first, to limit probing. Even so, a responder can learn what certificates an initiator will accept from CERTREQ payloads, and with EAP the responder proves its identity first.

Repeated rekeying through CREATE_CHILD_SA without new Diffie-Hellman exchanges leaves all SAs vulnerable if a single key is broken. Implementers should limit it, although the RFC sets no limit. A prf with output under 128 bits, such as 3DES-CBC, MUST NOT be used. Implementations MUST NOT negotiate NONE as the IKE integrity algorithm or ENCR_NULL as the IKE encryption algorithm. Diffie-Hellman group one is described as historic only. Exponents must be erased after use, and the security of the protocol depends on good random numbers.

The NAT detection hashes can be reversed by trying every IPv4 address, so IKE can leak internal addresses. EAP methods that do not generate a shared key are open to man-in-the-middle attacks and SHOULD be avoided. IP fragmentation of long messages can let attackers exhaust reassembly buffers, which using Hash and URL certificate encodings helps to avoid. IANA registries for exchange types, payload types, transforms, notify types and others were created, and changes require expert review.
sections.eli5: Even with a secret handshake, some details can leak, so be careful with weak passwords, tiny keys and poor random numbers. A good lock is only as strong as its weakest part.

fields.name: IKE_SA Initiator's SPI
fields.desc: Chosen by the initiator to identify the IKE_SA; MUST NOT be zero.

fields.name: IKE_SA Responder's SPI
fields.desc: Chosen by the responder; zero in the first message of the initial exchange.

fields.name: Next Payload
fields.desc: Type of the payload that follows the header.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Includes the Initiator, Version and Response bits.

fields.name: Message ID
fields.desc: Matches responses to requests and prevents replay.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of header plus payloads in octets.

items.desc: Authenticates both sides and creates the first CHILD_SA.

items.desc: Creates or rekeys a child SA or the IKE_SA.

items.desc: Deletes SAs, reports errors, checks liveness.
